item: The extraction lock has a live gauge: seconds held and thread-seconds waited are kept as cumulative totals, so an open hold, an open wait and a pass that never ends are all readable
summary: lock_stats recorded a hold only when it ENDED and the pass monitor resets the window every pass, so a crashed pass, a hang or an 85 s hold left nothing to read. lock_stats now also keeps two cumulative totals for the life of the process (seconds the lock was held, thread-seconds spent waiting for it) behind a private leaf lock that reset() does not touch, and live_reading() adds the part of a hold and of each wait still open at the instant of the reading, with holder_age_s and the number waiting. Both totals only grow, so the difference of two readings is exact for the interval between them. extract_article marks asking (first statement of the outer try, before the lock), holding (first statement inside the hold), released (first statement of the finally inside the hold; it returns the clock reading, which is the hold's end stamp, so the pass window and the gauge end a hold at the same instant) and, through record(), gave_up (unconditional and idempotent: it closes a wait that holding never closed). The clock is read under the gauge's lock so a held fraction can never exceed the elapsed time; every step body contains no call, so under CPython 3.13 an interrupt cannot land between two statements of one mark. A stale wait is closed at the thread's next ask and a phantom holder at the next hold taken by another thread, each keeping the totals continuous. Nothing reads the gauge yet (the monitor block waits for the governor PR). Proof: 23 tests, among them an eight-thread run checked against an independent log (a tape of the gauge's own clock reads, one labelled entry per mark, tolerance 1e-6) and AST pins that the marks sit where the exception table needs them and that no step body calls anything; 29 mutants, among them the three the independent read of the first head found surviving, all killed. An Opus read of the first head found five defects (a waiter leaked when an interrupt landed between asking and the lock, so waited_s went backwards; the phantom-holder edge stated too narrowly and since left set at depth 0; a 64 KB claim the first A/B contradicted; three surviving mutants and a positional tape; a cost apportioned rather than measured); all five are folded here. Signal probe against a stub body with an interrupt every 1 to 40 microseconds: 190,638 interrupts, 0 leaked waiters, 0 holds left set at depth 0, 11,929 (6.3 percent) phantom holders (an interrupt at a mark's own entry; inflated by construction, a real KeyboardInterrupt is one event). Cost, measured alone on the machine: the two marks inside the hold take about 1.2 microseconds (medians 1.22, 1.21, 1.22 microseconds on this machine; 1.1, 1.1, 1.7 on the first), all four marks 2.3 to 2.6 (2.1 to 3.0 on the first) against a 4.2 to 4.5 ms extraction of an 8 KB page on one thread (26 to 30 ms for 64 KB); shared vCPUs, noisy. In the real collector (run_scrape_once + EthicalFetcher + store + write gate over the in-process session double, zero network, SQLCipher, 14 collectors, lock on, pins trafilatura 2.1.0 / lxml 6.1.1, 4 shared vCPUs with the run pinned to two), base = main 4460855d0 against this head, five alternating runs per cell, median [min..max]: 8 KB pages 420 [412..442] articles/min on base against 424 [397..437] with the gauge, mean hold 39.8 against 40.4 ms, lock held share 28.4 against 28.0 percent; 64 KB pages 121 [116..126] against 120 [113..129] articles/min, mean hold 319 against 312 ms, mean wait 841 [790..919] against 872 [787..985] ms, held share 64.2 against 64.3 percent. Paired by run number (the two cells of a run ran back to back), fold over base: articles/min median 0.988 [0.964..1.048] at 8 KB and 0.988 [0.938..1.032] at 64 KB. No difference beyond the spread of five runs; throughput drifts down across the 64 KB runs on BOTH trees (base 126 to 116), so the order alternates and the pairs are the fair reading. Not clean, said plainly: the first A/B (the pre-fold gauge, three runs, an older base) read the longest single hold and longest single wait higher with the gauge at both sizes (8 KB: hold 0.75 against 0.56 s, wait 0.95 against 0.77 s; 64 KB: hold 2.74 against 2.66 s, wait 11.4 against 10.6 s) and an earlier draft of this row called that absent at 64 KB, which was wrong. In the second A/B on this head the longest hold reads lower with the gauge (8 KB 0.81 against 0.85 s, 64 KB 2.86 against 3.01 s) and the longest wait about equal (0.84 against 0.82 s, 12.2 against 11.9 s), paired medians 0.75 and 0.95 for the hold, 1.05 and 1.01 for the wait. Each is one event per run, so the direction is not reproduced and the first reading is INFERRED to be scheduler noise on shared vCPUs, not shown; a small effect on a single event is not excluded. Cross-check on the ten gauge runs of the second A/B: the gauge's growth over the measured passes equals the pass window's hold total to within 1.7 to 4.4 ms over totals of 26 to 251 s (the gauge starts a hold at the holding mark's own clock read, a few microseconds after the window's got stamp: 2 to 6 microseconds per hold over 720 holds, INFERRED from the size, not separately measured) and its wait total to within 2.2 ms over 69 to 709 s, with nobody waiting and no holder at the end of any run. Known edges, stated in the code: an unmatched release is clamped; an interrupt at a mark's own entry (frame start or call return) can still skip that mark; a skipped asking or holding leaves a waiter that record() and the next asking close; a skipped released leaves a holder that the next holding from another thread closes and that stays until restart when no other thread ever takes the lock. Best effort, never an extraction's result. Not measured: lock off, other core counts, a store with real article history, real network time; only 8 and 64 KB bodies.
